story.title: Spain's Parliament Rejects Housing Measures Amid Ongoing Protests
story.summary: Spain's minority government faced a setback as parliament rejected two emergency housing measures aimed at improving affordability. The decision followed widespread protests, sparked by a pensioner's eviction, with critics arguing that the proposed measures would exacerbate the housing market issues.

explore_lenses.label: What actually changed after the votes?
explore_lenses.title: Two emergency decrees were rejected
explore_lenses.summary: Spain’s lower house did not ratify either emergency housing decree, blocking the government’s immediate package on evictions, supply and lease stability. The measures had been approved by the cabinet days earlier and required congressional validation.

claims.text: The two measures were Real Decreto-ley 26/2026, covering protections tied to housing’s social function and affordable supply, and Real Decreto-ley 27/2026, covering stability in primary-residence leases.

The first decree included a temporary limit on certain home purchases through December 31, 2028, a temporary suspension regime for evictions of vulnerable people without alternative housing, tenant protections, rules for identifying large landlords, and tax measures.
The government’s other decree would have let residential tenants renew leases automatically; AP reported that it was intended to make leases automatically renewable by tenants.

explore_lenses.label: Why did Junts and other opponents vote no?
explore_lenses.title: Dispute centered on supply and legislative method
explore_lenses.summary: Junts argued the decrees would reduce rental supply and leave speculation insufficiently addressed, while the government argued they were necessary renter protections. The Popular Party and Vox also opposed both; some smaller parties split their votes and objected to governing by decree.

claims.text: Junts spokesperson Míriam Nogueras said the measures would prompt owners to withdraw homes from the rental market and raise prices; she also argued that they still allowed speculative purchases and evictions.

Junts submitted an alternative 59-page proposal that included tax changes, a voluntary lease extension rather than a mandatory one, limits on certain acquisitions by financial entities, investment funds and large landlords, and eviction protections in specified cases.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez said her ministry had incorporated 90% of Junts’s proposals and urged the party to support or abstain on the decrees.
The Basque Nationalist Party and Coalición Canaria backed the first decree but opposed the second, criticizing the use of decrees rather than legislation negotiated with other parties.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next for renters and the government?
explore_lenses.title: Fresh legislation is possible, but no agreed route exists
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate decrees failed, while renter activists planned further demonstrations. Junts has called for renewed negotiations around its alternative text, but reporting did not identify an agreed replacement timetable or a settled parliamentary majority.

claims.text: The renters’ association Sindicato de Inquilinas said it was calling for further protests on Saturday and advocating a general strike after the vote.
Junts urged the government to negotiate changes, while the government declined to withdraw the decrees before the vote.

AP reported that fresh legislation was one possible next step, but also that it was unclear how the government would proceed; Spanish media speculation about an early election had not been confirmed by Sánchez’s office.

story_report.summary: Spain’s parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees as housing protests continued, dealing the government a setback in its effort to address affordability and tenant protections. One measure combined restrictions on certain home purchases, eviction safeguards and tax provisions; the other would have allowed tenants to renew primary-residence leases automatically. The vote leaves those measures without parliamentary approval, while the government’s next legislative move remains unclear.

sections.heading: Housing decrees contained eviction and lease rules
sections.body: Real Decreto-ley 26/2026 addressed housing’s social function and affordable supply. Its provisions included a temporary limit on certain home purchases through December 31, 2028, a temporary suspension regime for evictions of vulnerable people without alternative housing, tenant protections, rules to identify large landlords and tax measures. Real Decreto-ley 27/2026 focused on stability in primary-residence leases and would have enabled automatic tenant renewals.

sections.heading: Junts and regional parties challenged decrees
sections.body: Junts spokesperson Míriam Nogueras said the measures would lead owners to remove homes from the rental market and raise prices, while still permitting speculative purchases and evictions. Those are stakeholder assessments rather than outcomes established by the vote. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez said the ministry had incorporated 90% of Junts’s proposals, but Junts sought further negotiations; the Basque Nationalist Party and Coalición Canaria also criticized using decrees instead of legislation negotiated with other parties.

sections.heading: Renters seek further housing protests
sections.body: The renters’ association Sindicato de Inquilinas said it was calling for further protests on Saturday and advocating a general strike after the vote. Junts had submitted an alternative proposal including tax changes, voluntary rather than mandatory lease extensions, limits on some acquisitions by financial entities, funds and large landlords, and specified eviction protections. AP reported that fresh legislation was one possible response, but the government’s course had not been determined.

unresolved.text: As of October 2, 2026, there was no confirmed replacement bill, date for another vote, or decision to call an early election.
